1 INTRODUCTION: Acclaimed as the third generation of artificial neural network (Maass, 1997), Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have brought brand-new inspiration in computational neuroscience. As the corresponding neuron fires spikes only when the current membrane potential exceeds the firing threshold, SNNs have the distinctive characteristics of binary output, high sparsity, and biological plausibility. Therefore, compared with traditional ANN models, SNNs can further improve computational efficiency and reduce power consumption, which facilitates its remarkable superiority in the application of neuromorphic chips (Merolla et al., 2014; Davies et al., 2018; DeBole et al., 2019). Considering that SNNs have not found an effective learning algorithm yet, ANN-SNN conversion and back-propagation through time (BPTT) are still the two most concerning training methods at present. Compared with BPTT, ANN-SNN conversion avoids the non-differentiable problem in the direct training procedure of SNNs and thus reduces the overall training complexity. ANN-SNN conversion aims to establish the mapping relationship between the activation output and average firing rate. Traditional conversion methods exploit larger time-steps to overcome the conversion error and thus achieve high performance (Diehl et al., 2015). Many of the following works have attempted to optimize the performance from multiple perspectives, including using the soft-reset mechanism (Han et al., 2020; Rueckauer et al., 2017), proposing more adaptive activation functions (Cao et al., 2015; Ho & Chang, 2021; Bu et al., 2022b), adopting a trainable threshold (Sengupta et al., 2019; Ding et al., 2021; Bu et al., 2022a), etc. But these strategies cannot effectively eliminate the error caused by the deviation between the actual and desired firing rate, especially when the number of time-step is small. Some recent works consider to compensate the errors by introducing burst spikes (Li & Zeng, 2022) and signed spiking neurons (Li et al., 2022). Unlike these works, our paper attempts to eliminate the error with vanilla spiking neurons and answer the question of where the extreme performance of ANN-SNN conversion is. In this paper, we observe and identify the source of the conversion error and propose an iterative optimization method based on shifting initial membrane potential, which can fulfill accurate mapping between ANNs and SNNs under ideal situation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1 We introduce the concept of offset spike to infer the deviation between the actual SNN firing rate and desired SNN firing rate. We point out that the case of firing one more (or less) spike is the main reason for conversion error. 2 We propose a method to judge the offset spike based on the residual membrane potential and an optimization method to eliminate the conversion error through shifting up or down the initial membrane potential. We derive the optimal shifting distance and prove that one spike can be increased or decreased under this condition. 3 We evaluate our methods on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet datasets. The proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art ANN-SNN conversion methods using fewer time-steps. For example, we achieve 67.12% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with only 6 time-steps (4 time-steps calibration and 2 time-steps inference). Moreover, it is worth noting that we have reached the same level of performance as BPTT under the condition of reducing memory and computing resources significantly. 4 We discover that our proposed method has an iterative property. Under an ideal situation, the deviation within the range of k spikes will be eliminated entirely after adopting our approach for k times. After 4 iterations, the mean-square error between actual and desired firing rate of the output layer can reach 0.001 for the ResNet-20 model on CIFAR-100. 2 RELATED WORKS: The principle of ANN-SNN conversion is to map the parameters from pre-trained ANN models to SNNs, which avoids training SNNs directly and reduces energy consumption significantly. (2020) adopted “reset-by-subtraction” mechanism, which alleviated the problem of information loss and improved the precision of conversion process effectively. For the setting of firing threshold, various strategies have been proposed, including RobustNorm (Rueckauer et al., 2017), SpikeNorm (Sengupta et al., 2019), adjustable threshold (Han et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021; Ho & Chang, 2021; Bu et al., 2022a;b), etc. Recently, spiking neural networks with high accuracy and low latency have become the focus and target of academic research. To reduce the time latency of the network, one must carefully deal with the exact spiking time of neurons. Deng & Gu (2021); Li et al. 1 INTRODUCTION: Acclaimed as the third generation of artificial neural network (Maass, 1997), Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have brought brand-new inspiration in computational neuroscience. As the corresponding neuron fires spikes only when the current membrane potential exceeds the firing threshold, SNNs have the distinctive characteristics of binary output, high sparsity, and biological plausibility. Therefore, compared with traditional ANN models, SNNs can further improve computational efficiency and reduce power consumption, which facilitates its remarkable superiority in the application of neuromorphic chips (Merolla et al., 2014; Davies et al., 2018; DeBole et al., 2019). Considering that SNNs have not found an effective learning algorithm yet, ANN-SNN conversion and back-propagation through time (BPTT) are still the two most concerning training methods at present. Compared with BPTT, ANN-SNN conversion avoids the non-differentiable problem in the direct training procedure of SNNs and thus reduces the overall training complexity. ANN-SNN conversion aims to establish the mapping relationship between the activation output and average firing rate. Traditional conversion methods exploit larger time-steps to overcome the conversion error and thus achieve high performance (Diehl et al., 2015). Many of the following works have attempted to optimize the performance from multiple perspectives, including using the soft-reset mechanism (Han et al., 2020; Rueckauer et al., 2017), proposing more adaptive activation functions (Cao et al., 2015; Ho & Chang, 2021; Bu et al., 2022b), adopting a trainable threshold (Sengupta et al., 2019; Ding et al., 2021; Bu et al., 2022a), etc. But these strategies cannot effectively eliminate the error caused by the deviation between the actual and desired firing rate, especially when the number of time-step is small. Some recent works consider to compensate the errors by introducing burst spikes (Li & Zeng, 2022) and signed spiking neurons (Li et al., 2022). Unlike these works, our paper attempts to eliminate the error with vanilla spiking neurons and answer the question of where the extreme performance of ANN-SNN conversion is. In this paper, we observe and identify the source of the conversion error and propose an iterative optimization method based on shifting initial membrane potential, which can fulfill accurate mapping between ANNs and SNNs under ideal situation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1 We introduce the concept of offset spike to infer the deviation between the actual SNN firing rate and desired SNN firing rate. We point out that the case of firing one more (or less) spike is the main reason for conversion error. 2 We propose a method to judge the offset spike based on the residual membrane potential and an optimization method to eliminate the conversion error through shifting up or down the initial membrane potential. We derive the optimal shifting distance and prove that one spike can be increased or decreased under this condition. 3 We evaluate our methods on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet datasets. The proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art ANN-SNN conversion methods using fewer time-steps. For example, we achieve 67.12% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with only 6 time-steps (4 time-steps calibration and 2 time-steps inference). Moreover, it is worth noting that we have reached the same level of performance as BPTT under the condition of reducing memory and computing resources significantly. 4 We discover that our proposed method has an iterative property. Under an ideal situation, the deviation within the range of k spikes will be eliminated entirely after adopting our approach for k times. After 4 iterations, the mean-square error between actual and desired firing rate of the output layer can reach 0.001 for the ResNet-20 model on CIFAR-100. 2 RELATED WORKS: The principle of ANN-SNN conversion is to map the parameters from pre-trained ANN models to SNNs, which avoids training SNNs directly and reduces energy consumption significantly. The primary target is to match the activation value of ANNs and average firing rate of SNNs. Cao et al. (2015) were the pioneers to do research in this field, and they replaced ReLU activation layers in ANNs with spiking neurons to fulfill the conversion procedure. Ho & Chang (2021); Bu et al. (2022b) proposed new activation functions, which better fit the finiteness and discreteness of the spike firing rate. Rueckauer et al. (2017); Han et al. (2020) adopted “reset-by-subtraction” mechanism, which alleviated the problem of information loss and improved the precision of conversion process effectively. For the setting of firing threshold, various strategies have been proposed, including RobustNorm (Rueckauer et al., 2017), SpikeNorm (Sengupta et al., 2019), adjustable threshold (Han et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021; Ho & Chang, 2021; Bu et al., 2022a;b), etc. Recently, spiking neural networks with high accuracy and low latency have become the focus and target of academic research. To reduce the time latency of the network, one must carefully deal with the exact spiking time of neurons. Deng & Gu (2021); Li et al. (2021) fine-tuned the bias in each layer under the uniform current assumption. Nevertheless, the actual current would never be distributed uniformly. In terms of expectation, Bu et al. (2022b) proved that one-half of the threshold is the optimal value for initial membrane potential, and charging this value can prompt neurons to spike more uniformly. However, as the authors pointed out: there is still a mismatch between ANN and SNN due to the so called “unevenness error”. In addition, other methods like burst spikes (Li & Zeng, 2022) and signed spiking neurons (Wang et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2022), have also been introduced to further improve the performance. These works aim to alleviate the conversion loss. However, they damaged the biological plausibility and binary property of spiking neurons. In addition to ANN-SNN conversion, back-propagation with exact spike time is another common way to train SNNs. Surrogate gradient (O’Connor et al., 2018; Zenke & Ganguli, 2018; Bellec et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018; 2019; Kim & Panda, 2020; Zenke & Vogels, 2021) has been widely used to tackle the non-differentiable problem in the training process, which substitutes the Heaviside function with a derivable function. With the help of the surrogate gradient, back-propagation through time enables the network to adjust weights by focusing every exact time-step. On this basis, Fang et al. (2021); Rathi & Roy (2021); Guo et al. (2022) further attempted the optimization of hyperparameters and gradient. Bohte et al. (2002); Kheradpisheh & Masquelier (2020); Zhang & Li (2020) proposed a timing-based learning method, which viewed the specific spike firing time as significant temporal information to transmit between layers. Still, this type of method only applies to shallow networks at present. In addition, hybrid training methods have attracted extensive attention recently. Wang et al. (2022b); Rathi & Roy (2021) combined ANN-SNN conversion with BPTT to obtain higher performance under low latency. Kim et al. (2020) adopted rate-coding and timecoding simultaneously to train SNNs with fewer spikes. Mostafa (2017); Zhou et al. One intuitive explanation is that higher initial membrane potential will make the spiking neurons fire earlier and increase the firing rates during the period [0, T ], while lower initial membrane potential will make the spiking neurons fire later and decrease the firing rates. By combining Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, we propose the complete spike calibration algorithm. Our method can be divided into two stages. Firstly, for l-th layer, we spend ρ time-steps to detect the specific spike firing situation.
